title: Methodus nova et facilis calculum variationum tractandi

deep.reconstruction:
This page is transitional. It finishes §30 and opens a new section, 'Dilucidationes super Theoria variationum ad functiones saltem unius variabilis accommodata'.

The method of E420 is to embed the extremal in a one-parameter family. For a double integral this means z = z(x, y, t), and the variation of ∬Z dx dy is dt times the t-derivative of the integral. On the previous pages (§29) Euler collected that variation for Z depending on z and its partial derivatives up to third order. It splits into two parts:
- a double integral of (∂z/∂t) times the Euler–Ostrogradsky expression N − ∂P/∂x + ∂²Q/∂x² − … − ∂P'/∂y + …;
- a large collection of single integrals, which are boundary terms.

In §30 and at the top of this page Euler confesses three things. He cannot yet see what these individual members mean or how they could be used. The subject needs much closer investigation, which can hardly begin until particular cases are worked out. Even the one-variable theory has not been made clear enough to grasp the 'true nature' of each part of the variation.

§31 states the general problem. Let y be any function of x and Z any expression in x, y and the differential ratios dy/dx, d²y/dx², and so on. If y is replaced by an infinitely close function, by how much does ∫Z dx increase or decrease? In modern terms this is the first variation δJ = J[y + εη] − J[y] to first order in ε.

§32 (continued on the next page) recasts this geometrically. Take a curve AM over the axis AP, with abscissa AP = x and ordinate PM = y, and let W = ∫Z dx along it. Take any neighbouring curve αμ. Its endpoints α and μ need not coincide with A and M, so endpoint variation is allowed. The difference between the two values of ∫Z dx is exactly the variation of W computed earlier by the parameter method. §33 then illustrates this with the brachistochrone functional ∫√(1+p²)/√x dx.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page; it contains only a programmatic statement and a problem formulation.

ideas.what: Interpretation of the variation δW as the first-order difference of the functional between a given curve and an arbitrary infinitely near curve, including displaced endpoints (α vs A, μ vs M).
ideas.modern_name: First variation of a functional with variable endpoints (general variation formula)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange (δ-method, 1755/1760) and Euler (E420, 1771/72); the systematic general variation formula is later textbook material
ideas.where_published: E420 itself (§§31–34 ff.); also Euler's Institutiones calculi integralis vol. III appendix (E385) on calculus of variations

ideas.what: Admission that the boundary (single-integral) terms in the variation of double integrals are not understood and require further study.
ideas.modern_name: Boundary terms / natural boundary conditions for multiple-integral variational problems (divergence theorem form)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Lagrange; Gauss (1830, capillarity); Poisson (1833); Ostrogradsky (1834–38); Sarrus (1842); Cauchy
ideas.where_published: E420 §30; discussed in Goldstine, A History of the Calculus of Variations (1980), and the Opera omnia I.25 editor's introduction (Carathéodory)

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a programmatic transition. Euler's acknowledgment that the double-integral boundary terms are not understood is an open thread, but it is well documented and was resolved in the 19th century (Ostrogradsky, Sarrus and others). The problem statement and geometric recasting are standard.
